$comment: Split out of 60-metals.json on 2026-10-04 (RELATIONS.md section 9, wave 0.7) so one agent can own one file. Balance: 103 judgement edges across 6 subtrees. The `metal` root in 60-metals.json references these by id.

roots.name: Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion
roots.description: Where the C64's aluminium comes from. Bauxite is dug, digested in caustic soda to alumina, and electrolysed in molten cryolite to 99.7% metal - about 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne, the largest single industrial electricity draw anywhere in this tree. The ingot is then DC-cast to a rolling ingot and rolled down to 6-25 um foil for the electrolytic capacitors in the power supply, to sheet for the case and shield cans, and extruded for the heat sinks. Note that the capacitor foil and the plain foil are different jobs for the same rolling mill.

facts.label: Typical chain
facts.value: ~1.5-2 t bauxite -> 1 t alumina -> 0.50-0.52 t aluminium

facts.label: Hall-Heroult energy
facts.value: 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne of aluminium; 1980s plants commonly ran 15,000-17,000

facts.label: Why the number has not moved
facts.value: 2.1 V theoretical cell voltage against 3.5-4.5 V in practice, and 80-90% current efficiency

roots.name: Sodium compounds: caustic soda and soda ash
roots.description: Sodium is not in the machine as a metal, but the C64 could not exist without it: caustic soda dissolves bauxite to make alumina, and the same chlor-alkali industry that makes the caustic soda also makes the chlorine and hydrogen that become the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Behind both sits a bed of rock salt or a bucket of evaporite from a solar salt pan.

roots.name: Tantalum powder for electrolytic capacitors
roots.description: A 1982 C64 has a no tantalum capacitors on the 250407 mainboard (alu+ceramics per repaired passives note), in the analogue filter section, and tantalum beads in small packages. Each one is a sintered porous tantalum anode with a tantalum oxide dielectric and a solid manganese dioxide or a liquid electrolyte. The tantalum metal is won from columbite-tantalite, a refractory oxide ore, through a hydrofluoric-acid digestion that is one of the most corrosive industrial processes in existence. In 1982-83 there was a real tantalum supply crisis - the Congo and Brazil supply, the Botswana and Zimbabwe expansions, the US stockpile, and a price that doubled - and it is the one place in this tree where a commodity shock from a mining country touched a home computer.

facts.label: Metal purity
facts.value: 99.9%+; capacitor powder is made from very high-purity metal

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: columbite-tantalite (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 at 10-40% Ta2O5

facts.label: Market 1982-83
facts.value: a genuine supply disruption in 1982-83; the price roughly doubled and the electronics industry began substituting niobium

facts.label: Capacitor grade
facts.value: capacitor-grade powder, 99.9%+ Ta, particle size controlled by milling and by sodium reduction

facts.label: Anodisation
facts.value: 2-4x formation voltage

facts.label: Counter-electrode
facts.value: MnO2 / conductive polymer

facts.label: In-1982
facts.value: capacitor-grade powder route

roots.note: Merged powder noted particle size 1-8 um vs anode 2-10 um (anode range kept); bipolar vs polarised (polarised kept); silver-electrode timing noted. Surviving handful-of-tantalum-caps corrected: 250407 uses alu+ceramics, NOT tantalum (repaired passives note kept).

roots.name: Manganese: the steel deoxidiser
roots.description: Manganese has no visible place in a C64, but without it the steel the case and the shielding are made from would have inclusions and blowholes in it. Almost all manganese ore is used to make ferromanganese, which is added to the steelmaking furnace as a deoxidiser and desulphuriser and as an alloying element. It is a branch included because the steel branch cannot honestly stop without it.

facts.label: Refined form
facts.value: ferromanganese, most commonly high-carbon at 6-8% C

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: pyrolusite MnO2 at 30-50% Mn; the 'manganese nodules' on the abyssal plains held most of the world's reserve

roots.name: Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain
roots.description: The bottom of the steel branch. Iron ore is dug, concentrated, reduced and never appears in a C64, and this branch exists so that the steel branch terminates in a mine rather than in an abstraction. The 1982 iron ore trade was dominated by three names: Mount Whaleback and the Pilbara in Western Australia, the Carajas and Quadrilatero Ferrifero in Brazil, and the Labrador Trough and the Mesabi range in North America. The ore is hematite, or magnetite, or both in a metamorphic banded iron formation - a rock that is 2 billion years old and was originally a chemical precipitate out of seawater.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 60-66% Fe for the Pilbara direct-shipment ore; 30-45% for the Mesabi taconite that had to be beneficiated

facts.label: Sulphur
facts.value: <0.05% for a good steelmaking ore; sulphur above 0.1% is a penalty

facts.label: World production 1982
facts.value: roughly 800-900 Mt of ore and concentrate

metal.soda-ash.name: Soda ash (Na2CO3)
metal.soda-ash.description: Sodium carbonate, the second half of the sodium story. It goes into glass (a huge 1980s user, though the glass agent owns that branch), into detergents, and into the Bayer plant as the carbonate that lime converts back into caustic. The Solvay process, still the dominant route in 1982, makes it from salt, limestone and coke in a solution-and-precipitation tower - no molten salt, no electrolysis.

facts.label: Solvay tower
facts.value: ~10 m diameter, 20-30 m tall, cooled to about -10 C at the top

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl, then 2 NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O

facts.label: Net
facts.value: 2 NaCl + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaCl2

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: order 1 t of CaCl2 brine per t of soda ash

metal.barite.drilling-mud.name: Drilling grade barite and its mud
metal.barite.drilling-mud.description: The larger half of the barite market, and the reason a chemical-grade barite supplier has to be selective. Drilling mud needs a barite that is dense, grindable to a very fine size, low in soluble salts and above all low in cadmium and other toxic heavy metals, because the drill cuttings go into a mud pit and the barite is not recovered. In 1982 the drilling grade specification was a gravity of at least 4.2 and a particle distribution such that 90% passed 45 um. A 1982 rig's mud for a deep well used 100-300 tonnes of barite per kilometre.

facts.label: Specification
facts.value: specific gravity above 4.2, 90% below 45 um, low soluble salts

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 100-300 t of barite per km of hole in a deep well

facts.label: Density
facts.value: 4.28 g/cm3 API-grade

metal.barite.drilling-mud.note: Medium confidence; the mud consumption figure is representative rather than a specific well. Merged rig barite noted nearly insoluble in water.

metal.barite.name: Barite (BaSO4) ore, 90-98%
metal.barite.description: Barite is a very heavy, very white, chemically inert mineral - specific gravity 4.5 - which occurs as veins, as replacement bodies in limestone, and as a residual clay. It has two completely separate markets. The drilling-mud market is by far the biggest and takes barite that has simply been crushed and graded to 200 mesh, because all it needs is density and a low quartz content. The chemical-grade market, which is where the barium titanate comes from, needs the barite to be low in iron and low in silica, because those impurities end up in the ceramic. In 1982 the chemical-grade barite was a small, carefully selected part of the output, and China and Morocco were the dominant suppliers.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 90-98% BaSO4 for drilling grade; chemical grade requires Fe2O3 <0.5% and SiO2 <1-2%

facts.label: Ba content
facts.value: 58.8% by mass

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: underground or surface; sometimes a byproduct of lead-zinc and of fluorspar

children.name: Barite vein and replacement mine
children.description: Barite is mined as a primary vein mineral - a gangue mineral of many lead-zinc hydrothermal deposits - or as a replacement of limestone. The processing is simple: crush, wash off the clay, and either float or just size and sell. A barite plant of the 1980s was a jaw crusher, a log washer and a deslimer, and the quality specification was almost entirely about the Fe2O3. The chemical-grade plants did a rougher job: a flotation and an acid leach to take the iron down.

facts.label: Processing
facts.value: crush to 25 mm, log wash, deslime, size to 200 mesh for drilling grade

facts.label: Chemical grade
facts.value: flotation plus an acid leach to bring Fe2O3 below 0.5%

children.note: Medium confidence on the chemical-grade processing route; it varies a lot by deposit.

metal.columbite.name: Columbite-tantalite concentrate
metal.columbite.description: A hard, black, sub-conchoidal mineral - (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 - that in practice is never a pure species but a solid solution, and that is the whole problem of the tantalum industry: tantalum and niobium are chemically almost identical and always occur together, with the tantalum content ranging from a few percent to more than 50% of the total. The separation is the entire industry. The main 1982 sources were the Greenbushes and Wodgina pegmatites in Western Australia, the Cat Creek and Oarkopper operations in Brazil, and the columbite-tantalite concentrates from the Congo, Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Tantalum-bearing tin slags from Malaysia and Brazil were a secondary source.

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 20-60% Ta2O5 in the tantalum-rich fraction; lower for ordinary columbite

facts.label: Host
facts.value: granitic pegmatite; the Greenbushes pegmatite is a lithium-tantalum-columbite body

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: the ore is chemically a refractory oxide locked in a silicate rock

children.name: Pegmatite open pit with sluicing
children.description: The tantalum ore is in a pegmatite dyke, a very coarse-grained granite intrusion, and the extraction in the small operations is almost artisanal: the dyke is blasted, the rock is crushed and hand-sorted, and the heavy tantalum minerals are concentrated on a sluice or a jig. The Greenbushes operation, at the time one of the largest, mined a 3 km pegmatite by open pit with a 200,000 t/year plant. So the tantalum in a 1982 C64's capacitors very plausibly came out of an Australian open cut in a pegmatite, hand-sorted and sluiced.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit, drill and blast, coarse crushing, hand sorting, gravity concentration, or a dense-medium plant

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: coltan at 20-30% Ta2O5 from a 0.05-0.1% Ta2O5 pegmatite

facts.label: Predecessor technology
facts.value: cassiterite and wolframite were the original 1940s products of these same operations

children.note: Greenbushes was already a tin mine before it was a tantalum mine and then a lithium mine - a genuinely rare example of one pit changing commodities. Medium confidence on the production figures for 1982.

metal.columbite.note: Merged columbite-ore noted placers/alluvial, Kivu/Rwanda-Burundi sources, cost-in-mining, coltan source and DRC timing; survivor grades kept.

metal.pegmatite-crystals.name: The crystals and the rare-metal pockets
metal.pegmatite-crystals.description: The leaf of the tantalum branch. A pegmatite is the last thing a granite magma crystallises, and because it is water-rich and volatile-rich it can hold elements that have no business being in a granite at all - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, tin, the rare earths - at hundreds of times their normal concentration. Those elements concentrate in the last pockets to crystallise, and a pocket 30 cm across can hold a few kilos of coltan worth more than the whole pegmatite around it. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor came out of small pockets in a last-stage granite pocket, hand-sorted out of a rock whose crystals are bigger than your fist, in a pegmatite that is less than 0.1% tantalum.

facts.label: Enrichment
facts.value: volatile elements concentrate in the final crystallising pockets, at 100-1000x background

facts.label: Pocket size
facts.value: cm to tens of cm, holding grams to kilograms of coltan

facts.label: Host
facts.value: a granitic pegmatite dyke

metal.barium-carbonate.name: Ceramic-grade barium carbonate
metal.barium-carbonate.description: A fine white powder, 99%+ BaCO3, and the actual commodity that the barium titanate maker buys. Its iron and sulphur contents are the specification that matters, and both come back from the reduction step. It is also used directly - in the glass frit of the ferrite coat, in the barium ferrite magnet, in the dielectric of the lower-value ceramic capacitor grades, and in the ferrite itself.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.0-99.5% BaCO3 for ceramic grade

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: BaTiO3, glass frit, ferrite, barium ferrite magnets

metal.hydrogen-sulfide.name: Hydrogen sulphide from the carbonation
metal.hydrogen-sulfide.description: The barium carbonate process makes hydrogen sulphide as a by-product, roughly 0.2 t of H2S per tonne of barium carbonate, and H2S is an acutely toxic gas that a 1982 barium plant either burned in a flare or sent to a Claus plant for elemental sulphur. It is also, if you are unlucky, a gas that kills by olfactory paralysis: at high concentration you cannot smell it, which is why a barium works had an H2S alarm on the roof and why the workers carried a supplied-air respirator. It is the least well-known hazard in this tree and a real one.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: roughly 0.15-0.3 t of H2S per tonne of BaCO3

facts.label: Control
facts.value: flared or sent to a Claus plant, with continuous monitoring

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: H2S paralyzes the sense of smell at high concentration

metal.hydrogen-sulfide.note: Medium confidence on the H2S yield; the hazard mechanism is textbook.

metal.columbite.tailings.name: Coltan tailings
metal.columbite.tailings.description: A coltan concentrator throws away over 99% of the mass it treats, and in the artisanal operations of the 1970s and 1980s that was put into the creek bed without any attempt at settling, and the creek carried it away. The ecological consequence of that was small compared to what followed - the coltan rush of 2000-2008 - but the mining itself was the problem and the tantalum industry spent most of the 1980s designing a better process and a better tailings facility precisely because it was planning for exactly the kind of scrutiny it eventually got. A node whose importance is only visible in hindsight.

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: over 99% of the feed mass, as a fine quartz-mica-feldspar slurry

metal.columbite.tailings.note: Low confidence; the 1980s artisanal tailings practice is poorly documented; this is reasoned from the mass balance rather than from a source.

metal.tantalum.thorium.name: Thorium in the coltan: a radioactive by-product
metal.tantalum.thorium.description: Columbite-tantalite carries thorium and uranium in solid solution, typically 0.01-0.5% Th as ThO2, and because thorium's chemistry is so close to the rare earths it follows them through the whole fluoride circuit and reports with the rare-earth product. It is an alpha emitter, so the refinery's thorium residue is a radioactive waste that has to be stored, and in 1982 the disposal arrangements in most producing countries were informal. The leaf is a radioactive waste site, which is a legitimate if slightly grim terminus for a branch of the metals tree.

facts.label: Thorium content
facts.value: 0.01-0.5% Th as ThO2 in coltan concentrate

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: follows the rare earths through the fluoride circuit

facts.label: 1982 handling
facts.value: thorium nitrate sold as a 'fertile material' for a thorium fuel cycle that never arrived; the rest was stored

metal.tantalum.thorium.note: The thorium content of coltan is well documented; medium confidence on the 1982 commercial handling arrangements.

metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source.name: Make ammonia from coke in the gasworks
metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source.description: In 1982 most ammonia in the soda industry still came from the gasworks: coke plus steam and iron passed over a hot carbonaceous catalyst, then cracked to nitrogen and hydrogen. Natural gas-based steam reforming had largely displaced this in North America and Western Europe, but coke-based ammonia remained standard in India, China and much of Eastern Europe - which is where much of the world's soda ash, and hence much of its glass, was made.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: iron promoted with K2O, or activated coke

metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source.note: Not established: that coke-oven gasworks were still the ammonia source for soda ash in 1982, the regional claim (India, China, Eastern Europe), or the ~1000 C and iron/K2O-catalyst figures. The Solvay chemistry recovers almost all its ammonia, so only the makeup supply is at stake.

metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln.name: The lime kilns that feed the Solvay tower
metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln.description: The Solvay process needs carbon dioxide and it gets it by burning limestone in a shaft kiln beside the tower, in the same way a sugar mill burns bagasse. The kiln gas, after the dust is knocked out and the gas is cooled and scrubbed, is about 40-45% carbon dioxide on a dry basis - lower than the 98% a dedicated CO2 plant would produce, but it came free with the lime the process also needed. The Solvay works was therefore a self-contained chemical plant that took limestone and salt and made soda ash, calcium chloride and CO2 in one site.

facts.label: Kiln
facts.value: shaft kiln, 1000-1100 C, beside the tower

facts.label: CO2 concentration
facts.value: 40-45% dry after dust removal

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: the lime itself, sold to steel and to agriculture

metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln.note: The Solvay reference gives the limestone calcination as 950-1100 C, not 1000-1100 C, and says nothing about a shaft-kill gas of 40-45% carbon dioxide. Not established: the dry CO2 concentration of the kiln gas.

metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.name: Causticise the spent brine to recover the salt
metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.description: The Solvay process does not consume the salt: the ammonium chloride in the spent brine is causticised with lime back to ammonia and sodium chloride, and the brine is re-saturated. The plant therefore closes its salt loop, and its only real consumption is limestone and energy and the ammonia. That closure is the whole reason Solvay was so cheap for a century and why it was so hard to displace until the chlor-alkali-soda ash route had caught up.

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NH3 + CaCl2 + 2H2O

facts.label: Re-saturation
facts.value: brine is re-saturated with mined salt and returned

metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.note: Medium confidence on the salt consumption figure; the chemistry is standard.

metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.name: Calcine the carbonate to a reactive powder
metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.description: The barium carbonate that comes out of the carbonation tank is 99.0-99.5% pure but coarse and dense, and barium titanate needs a reactive powder. So the carbonate is calcined at 1000-1200 C to break it down to the oxide and then re-carbonated lightly, or it is ground extremely fine. Either way it is a chemical-material step rather than a smelting one, and it is where a lot of the ceramic-grade versus technical-grade distinction is made.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: to raise the reactivity of the carbonate for the solid-state reaction with TiO2

metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.note: Medium confidence; the calcination step is standard but the specific practice varies.

children.name: Iron and sulphur in the ceramic grade
children.description: The ceramic-grade barium carbonate specification is essentially a statement about two impurities. Iron, carried through from the barite and from the flue of the reduction kiln, if it survives into barium titanate, acts as an acceptor and shifts the Curie point and the dielectric constant and hurts the loss - so iron has to be below a few hundred ppm. Sulphur, carried from the reduction and not removed by the carbonation, sits at the grain boundary of the fired ceramic and hurts the breakdown voltage. Both of them are the same answer as in the ferrite branch: wash, precipitate, and calcine in a controlled atmosphere. It is a recurring theme in ceramics that the last hundred ppm is the whole specification.

facts.label: Iron
facts.value: below a few hundred ppm; an acceptor dopant that degrades the dielectric

facts.label: Sulphur
facts.value: must be removed by the carbonation and the calcine; it degrades the breakdown voltage

children.note: Medium confidence; the impurity mechanisms in barium titanate ceramics are standard in the ceramics literature.

metal.barite.reduction.name: Barite to barium sulphide, then barium carbonate
metal.barite.reduction.description: The chemical reduction of barite. Barite plus coke at 900-1100 C in a rotary kiln gives barium sulphide: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO. That reaction needs about 1100 C to proceed at a useful rate, and the kiln is a long steel tube, 2-3 m diameter and 30-50 m long, rotating at 0.5-1 rpm, heated by a gas or oil burner at one end. The barium sulphide is leached out of the cooled cake with water, giving a solution of BaS, and that solution is carbonated with carbon dioxide - from a coke oven, from the sinter plant, from anywhere - and barium carbonate precipitates: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S. So the barium carbonate is made from a sulphate ore, a coke-oven gas and a stream of hydrogen sulphide, and the H2S is either burned to sulphur or sent to a Claus plant.

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO at 900-1100 C

facts.label: Kiln
facts.value: rotary, 2-3 m diameter, 30-50 m long, 0.5-1 rpm

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: the cake is leached with water, hot, and the BaS solution is clarified

facts.label: Carbonation
facts.value: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S, at room temperature

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~90% on the reduction, 95%+ on the carbonation

facts.label: Barium carbonate purity
facts.value: 99.0-99.5% for ceramic grade; iron is the impurity to watch

metal.tantalum.hf-digest.name: Hydrofluoric acid digestion at 100-200 C
metal.tantalum.hf-digest.description: The concentrate is digested in a mixture of hydrofluoric acid, nitric acid and hydrochloric acid at 100-200 C in a Teflon-lined or Monel vessel with a condenser to keep the HF in the loop. Ta2O5 and Nb2O5 both dissolve as pentafluorides, while iron, tin, thorium and most of the rare earths stay as insoluble fluorides or oxides and are filtered off. Thorium in particular is a problem: it is a radioactive alpha emitter that comes with the coltan and has to be separated and disposed of carefully. The mixed HF/HNO3/HCl digestion was the industry standard for decades; the Bayer process digest, using anhydrous HF with calcium fluoride at 150-200 C, arrived later.

facts.label: Medium
facts.value: HF/HNO3/HCl, or HF with CaF2 (the Bayer process digest)

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: Monel or Teflon-lined, with a reflux condenser - HF attacks glass

facts.label: Refractory waste
facts.value: 5-15% of the mass leaves as insoluble fluoride sludge; the hardest waste stream in the industry

metal.tantalum.hf-digest.note: The Bayer-process alternative digest came into commercial use in the 1980s and 1990s; the acid digestion below is the 1982 norm.

children.name: The fluoride digestion vessel
children.description: The digestor is the most aggressively corrosive piece of equipment in the metals tree. Anhydrous hydrofluoric acid at 100-200 C attacks glass, attacks most metals, and attacks concrete; so the vessel is Monel, nickel, or Teflon-lined, with the condenser and the piping also in Monel, and there is a continuous fluoride leak problem because HF is off-gassing from a boiling slurry. The industry answer through the 1980s was the Monel plant, with a steam stripping system to recover the HF and a caustic scrubber on the vent, and it was the single largest reason the industry needed a process chemist rather than a metallurgist.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: Monel, nickel, or PTFE-lined steel

facts.label: Why
facts.value: anhydrous HF at 100-200 C attacks glass, most metals and concrete

facts.label: Fluoride recovery
facts.value: steam stripping of the offgas, then a caustic scrubber

children.note: Medium confidence; the materials of construction for HF service are well established in chemical engineering handbooks.

metal.tantalum.separation.name: Separation of tantalum from niobium: K2TaF7
metal.tantalum.separation.description: From the fluoride solution the tantalum is selectively precipitated as potassium heptafluorotantalate, K2TaF7, by adding potassium chloride and hydrofluoric acid at 70-90 C - and this is the step that separates it from niobium, because K2TaF7 is far less soluble than K2NbF7. The K2TaF7 crystals are filtered, washed and dried. Then the metal is won from it in one of two ways. The potassium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with liquid potassium metal, or with sodium, at 700-800 C, giving a coarse tantalum powder. The aluminium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with aluminium in an induction furnace, and the charge is self-separating by particle size - the tantalum comes out as the finer powder and the aluminium-fluoride slag on top. The capacitor industry wanted the sodium-reduction powder specifically, because it could be made much finer.

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: K2TaF7 from the fluoride solution by KCl at 70-90 C; niobium stays in solution

facts.label: Potassium/sodium reduction
facts.value: K2TaF7 + 7Na -> Ta + 7NaF at 700-800 C; the standard capacitor-grade route

facts.label: Aluminium reduction
facts.value: K2TaF7 + 5Al -> Ta + 5AlF3, at 700-900 C in an induction furnace

facts.label: Product form
facts.value: tantalum powder; capacitor grade needs a controlled particle size and a high surface area

metal.tantalum.separation.note: The sodium reduction of K2TaF7 at 700-800 C is the standard capacitor-grade route and is still the industrial norm; the aluminium reduction is for bulk metal. Merged ore-to-powder noted Cu-reduction and salt-melt variants; K2TaF7 at 70-90 C kept (loser K2Ta2O7 claim not adopted). Loser pass-commentary dropped per CHECKLIST 7a.

children.name: Recycling the potassium and fluorine
children.description: The potassium in K2TaF7 and the fluorine in it both come back. The mother liquor from the precipitation is evaporated and the potassium is recycled, and the fluoride is recovered from the aluminium fluoride slag in the metal reduction by hydrolysing it to fluoride and re-fluorinating. A modern tantalum plant's fluorine and potassium consumption is a small fraction of its theoretical requirement because of this loop, and the 1980s plants were learning it. It is a small detail that says something about how tight the tantalum business economics were - and the answer is that they were tight enough to make the 1982-83 supply crisis severe.

facts.label: Streams
facts.value: KCl from the mother liquor; fluoride from the AlF3 slag

children.note: Low confidence on the 1982s recovery efficiencies; the flowsheet is standard but the plant data is proprietary.

metal.columbite.concentrator.name: Coltan concentrator: gravity, magnet and electrostatic
metal.columbite.concentrator.description: The coltan upgrade in a small operation is a classic three-stage gravity and magnetic plant: a shaking table or a jig throws away the quartz and mica, a magnetic separator takes off the magnetite and ilmenite, and a second gravity stage with a dense-medium separator makes a 20-30% Ta2O5 concentrate from a 0.05-0.1% pegmatite. Electrostatic separation takes out the zircon. The mass yield is under 1%, so the concentrator's job is mostly to throw away 99.5% of the rock, which is why a coltan operation is a small, cheap, labour-intensive plant sitting next to the pit rather than a large mill.

facts.label: Stages
facts.value: jig or shaking table, magnetic separator, dense medium, electrostatic

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: 0.05-0.1% Ta2O5 pegmatite

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 20-30% Ta2O5, at 60-80% recovery

metal.columbite.concentrator.note: Recovery figures for artisanal coltan operations vary enormously; medium confidence.

metal.manganese.ladle-charging.name: Charge the ferromanganese into the steel ladle
metal.manganese.ladle-charging.description: A ladle of steel is a bad place to drop a lump of ferromanganese, because the lump floats, the reaction is violent and the steel is left with unreacted alloy inclusions. So the FeMn is added in sized lumps and, increasingly in the 1980s, in cored wire - a steel tube filled with powdered ferromanganese and flux, fed into the ladle on a lance and dissolved by the passage of the steel through it. Cored-wire charging was a genuine 1980s development in secondary metallurgy and it improved the yield of the manganese, because it puts the metal into the steel rather than onto it.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sized lumps, or cored wire on a ladle lance

facts.label: Why
facts.value: a lump floats and reacts only at the surface; cored wire dissolves below the surface and gives a higher yield

facts.label: Typical addition
facts.value: order 1 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel

metal.manganese.ladle-charging.note: Medium confidence; cored-wire charging of ferroalloys is well documented in secondary-metallurgy practice.

metal.barite.rock.name: Barite vein in limestone or as a hydrothermal gangue
metal.barite.rock.description: The leaf: white bladed or massive barite filling a fracture, or replacing a fossiliferous limestone bed. The barite has essentially no use as a rock - it is only ever interesting where it happens to be 90% or better and low in iron.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: hydrothermal vein or replacement body in carbonate rock

metal.barite.mud-system.name: Barite, bentonite and lime: the drilling mud system
metal.barite.mud-system.description: A drilling mud is not one material; it is a designed composite. The barite is the weight - it is the only cheap, abundant mineral dense enough to hold back formation pressure at a density of 1.5-2.0. The bentonite is the viscosity and the filtration control, and it works because its sodium montmorillonite swells in water to several times its dry volume. The lime and the lime-soil inhibitors control the calcium contamination that comes up with the cement and that would flocculate the bentonite. So the barite branch of this tree converges with the bentonite branch of the steel branch, and both converge on the drilling of the oil and gas wells that produce the crude oil the plastics agent starts from.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: barite takes the mud to 1.5-2.0 specific gravity

facts.label: Viscosity
facts.value: bentonite, swollen to several times its dry volume

facts.label: Calcium control
facts.value: lime and inhibitors, because calcium flocculates the clay

metal.barite.mud-system.note: Medium confidence; the mud chemistry is standard drilling engineering.

metal.columbite.pegmatite.name: Granitic pegmatite dyke
metal.columbite.pegmatite.description: The leaf: a coarse-grained, quartz-feldspar-mica rock so coarse that individual crystals are centimetres across, with the tantalum-bearing minerals in small pockets of rare-metal enrichment. Pegmatites are the last-crystallising fraction of a granite magma, so they are the natural home of every incompatible element - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, rare earths. There is no more apt end point for the tantalum chain than a dyke of crystals bigger than your fist.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: granitic pegmatite: quartz, albite, potassium feldspar, mica, with coltan pockets

facts.label: Grain size
facts.value: commonly 1-100 mm crystals

metal.nickel-monel.name: Monel: nickel with copper
metal.nickel-monel.description: The alloy that made the fluorine chemistry of the 1980s possible: 60-70% nickel with 30% copper, and sometimes molybdenum, made in the same vacuum-melted, cast-and-rolled route as any nickel alloy. Monel resists hydrofluoric acid better than almost anything because the nickel fluoride film that forms is protective while aluminium fluoride and steel fluoride are not. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor was separated in a vessel made of a nickel alloy that came out of the nickel branch of this same file, and the aluminium capacitor in the power supply is made with an acid that would destroy it.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 60-70% Ni, 25-35% Cu, sometimes 1-5% Mo

facts.label: Why it survives HF
facts.value: the nickel fluoride film is protective; aluminium and iron fluorides are not

metal.nickel-monel.note: Medium confidence; Monel's composition is well documented and the mechanism is the standard explanation.

metal.soda-ash.ammonia.name: Carbonation tower and the rotary calciner
metal.soda-ash.ammonia.description: A 20-30 m steel tower with a conical bottom, fed at the top with ammoniated brine and in the side with CO2 from the lime kilns. Sodium bicarbonate precipitates as a fine white slurry in the upper third and settles into the cone; the temperature is held near 40 C because below that the ammonium chloride in the liquor crystallises out and fouls the tower. Bicarbonate is then calcined at 200-250 C in a rotary kiln to soda ash.

facts.label: Tower temperature
facts.value: near 40 C at the precipitation zone

facts.label: NH3 loss
facts.value: order 0.1-0.3 t ammonia per t of soda ash, mostly vented

metal.soda-ash.ammonia.note: Tower internals varied; the conical settler is universal.
